alt: A general point, “questionnaires are cheap”, becomes application when it names the topic, the group and the issue: a questionnaire about income may suffer from social desirability because people under-report or exaggerate earnings.
caption: Name the topic, the group and the issue in every evaluation point.

alt: Social class can be operationalised by an occupational scale such as NS-SEC, by income and wealth, or by subjective class. Each has validity problems: occupational scales miss people without jobs and the very rich, income data may be refused or inaccurate, and subjective class captures identity rather than position.
caption: How class is measured changes who ends up in which class.

alt: An illustrative sample of 200 dots in which only a handful belong to one combined subgroup, such as working-class women from one minority group: too few to analyse reliably. So researchers need large, stratified or multistage samples, then qualitative interviews to show how combined disadvantages are experienced.
caption: Combined groups get small fast, so samples must be large and stratified.

alt: Retrospective questions ask people to look back, for example at a parent’s job when they were 14: cheaper but reliant on memory. Longitudinal cohort studies, such as the National Child Development Study of people born in 1958, follow the same people forward: more valid but expensive, and participants drop out.
caption: Look back cheaply, or follow forward validly but at a cost.

alt: Three ethical issues in researching children: informed consent from child and parent or guardian, the power imbalance between adult and child, and wellbeing if harm is revealed. Practical alternatives include observation in schools or play settings, short group interviews and simple activities.
caption: Consent, power and wellbeing shape every study involving children.

alt: Six crime types matched to the best measure and the reason: burglary and vehicle crime to police statistics with victim surveys; domestic abuse to confidential victim surveys; drug use to self-report studies; corporate crime to court and regulatory records; cybercrime to victim surveys and bank data; state crime to documents, journalism and testimony.
caption: The best measure depends on the type of crime.

after: ## Worked example: an extended response plan
alt: A four-part plan on victim surveys and gender: strengths (hidden crime such as domestic abuse, large samples, trends), limitations (trust, unreachable victims, memory, not defining experiences as crime), methods fixes (confidential self-completion, trained interviewers, triangulation) and a judgement.
caption: Strengths, limitations, a methods fix, then a judgement.
